node.label: Mary L. Dudziak
node.date_label: Desegregation as a Cold War Imperative (1988) · Cold War Civil Rights (2000) · Exporting American Dreams (2008) · War Time (2012)
node.description: In Cold War Civil Rights: Race and the Image of American Democracy (2000), Mary L. Dudziak argued that international criticism of American racism helped move the federal government toward civil rights reform. The Cold War also limited reform: anticommunism marginalized broader challenges to racial and economic inequality, while concern for national prestige could favor appearances over substantive change. Eric Arnesen’s 2002 review praised the account of federal image management but asked for stronger evidence of its effects on overseas audiences and closer analysis of the political alternatives being suppressed. Exporting American Dreams (2008) followed Thurgood Marshall between American civil rights and Kenya’s constitutional transition. War Time (2012) questioned the assumption that war is a temporary exception, arguing that this framing licenses extraordinary powers amid persistent military engagement. Eric A. Posner’s 2012 review disputed the empirical support for linking expectations of temporary war to acceptance of curtailed liberties. Dudziak’s work joins legal, African American and international history through specific connections between domestic institutions and global politics.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Desegregation as a Cold War Imperative” (1988); Cold War Civil Rights: Race and the Image of American Democracy (2000; new preface 2011; 25th anniversary edition 2025); September 11 in History: A Watershed Moment? (editor, 2003); Legal Borderlands (co-editor with Leti Volpp, special issue 2005; book reissue 2006); Exporting American Dreams: Thurgood Marshall’s African Journey (2008; revised paperback 2011); War Time: An Idea, Its History, Its Consequences (2012); Making the Forever War (co-editor with Mark Philip Bradley, 2021).
node.scope_note: Selected passages of the published 2010 essay, the 2012 War Time introduction, the 2012 IAS essay, the 2013 Mazower review and an authorized 2025 Cold War Civil Rights excerpt read. Arnesen’s review and Posner’s review read; Farber and Kohn available only as displayed extracts. Books and edited collections not read in full. Substantive Armitage response and Curtis Bradley review remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Idea of Wartime” (2012), Dudziak extends Lynn Hunt’s example in Measuring Time, Making History (2008) of historical actors excusing their actions through their era to American justifications of wartime conduct.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: IAS essay, paragraph beginning 'The idea that wartime is exceptional': Hunt's phrase 'a new kind of determinism' introduces the Barère example that Dudziak then applies to war. Hunt's book not independently read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hunt: time as an excuse for action

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Law, War, and the History of Time” (2010), Dudziak uses Durkheim’s account of socially produced temporal categories to question whether wartime is a natural division of history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read search-indexed excerpts of the journal/library PDF, Law, War, and the History of Time (2010), pp. 1672 and 1675, especially the body paragraph beginning Emile Durkheim noted and nn. 24–27. Durkheim is an explicitly named premise for treating temporal categories as socially produced; the essay then uses this premise to question wartime’s supposedly essential character. Part of the explanation is mediated through Carol Greenhouse. This is a local argumentative use, not a general or career-wide intellectual debt. The cited Durkheim edition is the 1976 translation; original unread. Direct PDF retrieval returned 403; the present check is limited to the indexed page excerpts.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Law, War, and the History of Time” (2010), Dudziak questions framing persistent American warfare as exceptional time, contrasting Agamben’s state-of-exception formulation with wartime law as ordinary practice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Published essay p. 1670, opening discussion and nn. 1–2, juxtaposes Agamben with 'the longstanding persistence of war'. A bounded objection to this framing, not a rejection of his entire project; Agamben's text unread independently.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Idea of Wartime” (2012), Dudziak uses Benedict Anderson’s concept of simultaneity to explain shared national feeling produced by watching the September 11 attacks unfold on television.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: IAS essay, paragraph beginning 'September 11, 2001': expressly calls the experience 'simultaneity' in Anderson's terms. Documents this application only; neither direct personal contact nor independent reading of Anderson's book is asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Nations United?” (2013), Dudziak praises Governing the World (2012) but argues that Mazower underexplains how contemporary international law can enable warfare as well as constrain it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Opening assessment and final section, especially paragraphs beginning 'At this point' and 'Following the path of lawfare': law becomes a 'technology of warfare'. Review read; Mazower's book not independently read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Mazower: law as a technology of warfare

proposed_edges.relationship: Cold War Civil Rights (2000) explains federal responses to Black freedom struggles through the international costs of American racism, while showing how anticommunism narrowed the scope of reform.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authorized 2025 excerpt, closing paragraphs beginning 'Yet the Cold War' and 'The narrow boundaries'; Arnesen (2002), pp. 243–245, identifies the contribution and questions evidence of overseas effects. Full book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Civil rights reform and its Cold War limits

proposed_edges.relationship: Exporting American Dreams (2008) follows Thurgood Marshall's work in Kenya to examine the limits of individual-rights-based law in inscribing equality; Farber's 2013 review places it where diplomatic and African American history meet.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Named mediation: Farber (2013), publisher-displayed extract, paragraphs beginning 'Back in 1996' and 'Compared to her first book'; explicitly places the books between diplomatic and African American history. Full book and full review unread; a specific connected history, not world-scale synthesis.
proposed_edges.map_label: Marshall, Kenya and the limits of law

proposed_edges.relationship: War Time (2012) makes the presumed temporariness of war a historical problem, examining how it justifies exceptional powers despite continuing American military involvement.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Book introduction pp. 3–9 read; Kohn (2013), publisher-displayed extract's opening paragraphs, places this intervention alongside military historians' understanding of persistent war. Full book and full review unread; contribution concerns war's legal and political framing.

proposed_edges.relationship: At the 2017 Grotius Lecture, David Armitage acknowledged that Mary L. Dudziak’s War Time: An Idea, Its History, Its Consequences (2012) inspired his Civil Wars: A History in Ideas (2017), according to Amy Flick’s contemporaneous conference report.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the report’s opening three prose paragraphs and contextual discussion. This is an acknowledgment reported by a conference observer, not a quotation independently checked against the lecture recording or either book. The official professional-association publication carries Flick’s original report. The journal text remains unread beyond its displayed extract and references.
proposed_edges.map_label: Armitage acknowledges War Time as an inspiration
